name: Socrates
info: Socrates (c. 470–399 BCE) was an Athenian philosopher who wrote nothing and is known through the accounts of Plato, Xenophon and others; he was tried for impiety and corrupting the youth and put to death by hemlock.

facts.born: 470 or 469 BCE in the Athenian deme of Alopece, an Athenian citizen; son of Sophroniscus, a stoneworker, and Phaenarete, a midwife
facts.died: 399 BCE in Athens, by drinking hemlock after being sentenced to death for impiety and corrupting the young; according to the Phaedo, his last words concerned a rooster owed to Asclepius
facts.role: Athenian philosopher; soldier in three campaigns of the Peloponnesian War, according to Plato; held no office and never ran for one
facts.known: the Socratic method of questioning (elenchus); his claim of ignorance; the search for definitions of the virtues; the view that virtue is knowledge; his trial and death; his influence on Plato and on later schools

t: Socrates wrote no texts and is known mainly through his pupils Plato and Xenophon, the comic dramatist Aristophanes and Aristotle, whose often contradictory accounts make up what is called the Socratic problem.

He questioned Athenians who were thought to be experts, showed that their definitions of virtues such as courage and justice contradicted themselves, and said that he was sure only that he did not know.

In 399 BCE a jury of hundreds of male citizens found him guilty of impiety and of corrupting the youth, and he drank hemlock after refusing his friends' offer to help him escape; scholars still disagree about why he was convicted.
dyk: Of all the works written about Socrates' trial, only three survive: Plato's Apology, Xenophon's Apology and Xenophon's Memorabilia.
ev: Born in the Athenian deme of Alopece to Sophroniscus and Phaenarete, in 470 or 469 BCE
The Thirty Tyrants begin to rule Athens; under them Socrates and four others are told to arrest Leon the Salaminian, and Socrates alone refuses, according to Plato's Apology
An amnesty is granted to Athenian citizens to prevent civil war after the fall of the Thirty

Accused by Meletus, Anytus and Lycon of impiety and corrupting the youth, he is tried before a jury of hundreds of citizens, sentenced to death, and drinks hemlock after refusing an escape offered by his friends
Friedrich Schleiermacher's essay on the worth of Socrates as a philosopher attacks Xenophon's accounts, and the attack is widely accepted
Nietzsche's The Birth of Tragedy holds Socrates responsible for the deterioration of ancient Greek civilisation

sections.early:
Socrates was born in 470 or 469 BCE in the Athenian deme of Alopece, to Sophroniscus, a stoneworker, and Phaenarete, a midwife. He was an Athenian citizen, born to relatively affluent parents. He lived close to his father's relatives and inherited, as was customary, part of his father's estate, which secured him a life reasonably free of financial concerns.

His education followed the laws and customs of Athens. He learned the basic skills of reading and writing and, like most wealthy Athenians, received extra lessons in gymnastics, poetry and music. He was married twice, though which marriage came first is not clear: his marriage to Xanthippe took place when he was in his fifties, and another marriage was to a daughter of Aristides, an Athenian statesman. He had three sons with Xanthippe.

He served in the Peloponnesian War and, according to Plato, distinguished himself in three campaigns. Everything known about him comes from the accounts of others: mainly Plato and Xenophon, who were both his pupils; Aristophanes, his contemporary; and Aristotle, who was born after his death. These sources are known to contradict one another.
sections.rise:
Socrates held no office and never ran for one, and he did not suggest any legislation. By the age of 45 he had already captured the interest of Athenians as a philosopher. He attracted great interest from the Athenian public and especially from Athenian youth, and he spent his time conversing with citizens, among them powerful members of Athenian society, scrutinising their beliefs and bringing the contradictions of their ideas to light.

He was notoriously ugly, with a flat turned-up nose, bulging eyes and a large belly, and his friends joked about his appearance. He was indifferent to material pleasures, including his own appearance and personal comfort. He neglected personal hygiene, bathed rarely, walked barefoot and owned only one ragged coat. He moderated his eating, drinking and sex, although he did not practise full abstention.

Politically, he did not take sides in the rivalry between the democrats and the oligarchs in Athens; he criticised both. As a citizen he abided by the law and carried out his military duty by fighting wars abroad. His aim was to help the city flourish by improving its citizens, for politics was, in his view, about shaping the moral landscape of the city through philosophy rather than through electoral procedures.
sections.deeds:
Socrates left no writings, so his method and ideas are known through Plato's dialogues above all. The Socratic method, or elenchus, typically begins when he asks a supposed expert for a definition of a subject, such as virtue, goodness, justice or courage. As he asks more questions, the interlocutor's answers eventually contradict the first definition, and the conclusion is that the expert did not really know it in the first place. Socrates also tests his own opinions in this way and does not teach a fixed doctrine.

He often claimed to be aware of his own lack of knowledge. The saying "I know that I know nothing" is often attributed to him on the basis of a statement in Plato's Apology. In some dialogues, however, he appears to credit himself with some knowledge. Gregory Vlastos distinguished two senses of knowledge in his speech, one certain and one derived from elenchus, though not all scholars agree with this.

His moral thought held that all virtues are essentially one, since they are a form of knowledge, and that a person is not good because they lack knowledge. In Plato's Protagoras he implies that "no one errs willingly". He also said that he heard a daimonion, an inner voice that deterred him from a course of action but never gave positive advice.
sections.opponents:
Socrates was a polarising figure in Athenian society. In The Clouds, Aristophanes presented a caricature of him that leaned towards sophism, ridiculing him as an absurd atheist; it is not clear whether this work is useful in reconstructing the historical Socrates. His religious views were also a source of friction: he rejected the anthropomorphism of traditional Greek religion by denying that the gods did bad things as humans do, and he seemed to believe in a daimonion of divine origin.

In 399 BCE Meletus, a poet, brought the accusation, and Anytus and Lycon joined him as accusers. The charges were corrupting the youth and asebeia, impiety: worshipping false gods and failing to worship the gods of Athens. The climate was politically tense. After the Athenian defeat at Aegospotami in 404 BCE, the Spartans replaced the democracy with the pro-oligarchic Thirty Tyrants, whom democrats later overthrew. It was true that Socrates did not stand for democracy under the Thirty and that most of his pupils were against the democrats.

Later writers also attacked him. The Epicureans criticised his belief in his daimonion and his regard for the oracle at Delphi, and the Pyrrhonists accused him of mock humility. Plato's Apology gives his defence: he had never corrupted anyone intentionally, and in condemning him, Athens itself would be the greatest loser.
sections.last:
Socrates was tried in late spring or early summer 399 BCE, and the trial likely went on for most of one day. He was found guilty by a majority vote of a jury of hundreds of male Athenian citizens. According to the custom, he proposed his own penalty. Plato has him suggest free food and housing at the state's expense for his services to the city or, more in earnest, a fine of one mina of silver, which according to him was all he had; Xenophon says he made no proposals. The jurors ordered the death penalty. He did not ask permission to go into exile.

He warned the jurors and the Athenians that criticism of them by his many disciples was inescapable, unless they became good men. After a delay caused by Athenian religious ceremonies, he spent his last day in prison among friends and followers, who offered him a chance to escape; he refused. He died the next morning by drinking hemlock. According to Plato's Phaedo, his last words were: "Crito, we owe a rooster to Asclepius. Don't forget to pay the debt."

Scholars disagree about why he was convicted, and there are two main theories. The first is that he was convicted on religious grounds, the second that the reasons were political. A more recent interpretation combines them, arguing that religion and state were not separate in ancient Athens.
sections.legacy:
With the exception of the Epicureans and the Pyrrhonists, almost all philosophical currents after Socrates traced their roots to him: Plato's Academy, Aristotle's Lyceum, the Cynics and the Stoics. Since he had not handed them an answer to questions such as the purpose of life, the schools diverged greatly in their readings of him. He was considered to have shifted the focus of philosophy from the natural world to human affairs. His pupils Euclid of Megara, Aristippus and Antisthenes drew differing conclusions and followed independent paths.

Muslim scholars translated Plato's works on Socrates into Arabic and admired him for combining his ethics with his lifestyle. In the early Italian Renaissance, Leonardo Bruni and Giannozzo Manetti presented a civic Socrates as a humanist and supporter of republicanism, while Marsilio Ficino drew parallels between his life and that of Jesus Christ.

Hegel held that Socrates marked a turning point through the principle of free subjectivity, yet justified the Athenian court. Kierkegaard considered Socrates his teacher and argued that he was purely an ironist. Nietzsche held him responsible for the deterioration of Greek civilisation, though the current mainstream view is that Nietzsche was ambivalent. After the Second World War, Hannah Arendt, Leo Strauss and Karl Popper saw him as an icon of individual conscience, and Popper contrasted Socratic individualism with Plato's ideas.

summary: Socrates (c. 470–399 BCE) was an Athenian philosopher who wrote nothing, so that his thought is known through Plato, Xenophon and others. He questioned Athenians about virtue and claimed ignorance, and in 399 BCE he was convicted of impiety and corrupting the youth and executed with hemlock.

W. K. C. Guthrie, A History of Greek Philosophy: Volume 3, The Fifth Century Enlightenment, Part 2, Socrates (Cambridge University Press, 1972)
Gregory Vlastos, Socrates, Ironist and Moral Philosopher (Cornell University Press, 1991)
C. C. W. Taylor, Socrates: A Very Short Introduction (Oxford University Press, 2019)
notes: Birth: the article gives c. 470 in the lead and 470 or 469 BCE in Biography; start is -470 with circa true.

The article contradicts itself on Socrates' politics only as a stated debate (leaning democratic or oligarchic); the life section leaves that out apart from the article's statement that he criticised both sides.
Event 1818 and 1872 are posthumous scholarly events, given because the article dates them; events 1 to 6 are of the life. The 'c. 470 BCE' label follows the lead.
The 403 BCE amnesty is in the article as a fact about Athens, not about Socrates; kept as context in the key events.
Aristophanes' The Clouds is not dated in the article, so it has no key event.
Plato's Apology is the source of the refusal to arrest Leon; Plato's Apology and Xenophon differ on his counter-proposal; both are given.
Left out: homosexuality and love discussion (Alcibiades, Diotima/Aspasia), the Euthyphro dilemma, detailed Socratic irony, eudaimonism, the liberalism and civil disobedience readings.
